openers.other-soil-types: Not every soil fits neatly into the great classification systems, and this chapter gathers the ones worth knowing anyway. It begins with peat, partly decayed vegetation that piles up in bogs, moors and other waterlogged ground where acidic, oxygen-poor, waterlogged conditions stop plants from rotting fully. Layer by layer, peat keeps a record of past vegetation and people, yet it can be drained for farming, cut and dried as fuel, worn into overhanging banks, or set smouldering underground by fires that light rain cannot put out. Then come soils named for their rock, climate or makers: an uncommon soil weathered from serpentine-bearing ultramafic rock, the fertile {{ref:soil-class-048}} of humid temperate lands, the shallow, humus-rich {{ref:soil-class-050}} on carbonate rock, and {{ref:soil-class-053}}, a dark Amazonian soil that people built with the help of {{ref:soil-class-083}}.

soil-class-070.title: Peat, the half-rotted store of the world's soil carbon
soil-class-070.text: Peat covers just 3% of the land surface, yet it stores up to 550 Gt of carbon. That is 42% of all the carbon held in soils, more than all other vegetation on Earth, forests included. Peat is an accumulation of partly decayed vegetation and organic matter, found in bogs, moors and other waterlogged ground. Sphagnum, or peat moss, is one of its commonest parts, though many other plants contribute. It forms in wet places where flooding or stagnant water cuts off oxygen and slows decomposition. Soils made mainly of peat are {{ref:soil-class-098}}. The world holds about 4 trillion cubic meters of it. Estimates of its share differ: Joosten and Clarke say peat-covered land holds one third of the carbon in the world's soils. In principle peat is renewable. In practice it regrows only about 1 mm a year, and only in 30–40% of peat areas, far slower than industrial extraction. Over geological time it is often the first step toward coal, especially low-grade lignite. Centuries of burning and draining peat have released much CO2, adding to human-caused climate change. Engineers see a different problem. Highly organic peat consolidates poorly, so it makes an unstable foundation for roads and buildings.

soil-class-074.title: Draining peat lets ancient carbon escape
soil-class-074.text: Under water, peat gathers organic carbon for thousands of years. Drainage opens that store to the air. Peat drainage is the draining of peat soils, often through canals, for agriculture, forestry and peat extraction. Once exposed, the carbon decomposes to CO2. About 12% of the world's peat areas have been drained and damaged. As of 2022 they emitted an estimated 4% of human-made greenhouse gases, before counting fires. England's peat stores 584 million tonnes of carbon, but they release around 11 million tonnes of CO2 a year through damage and draining. The Netherlands shows the long-term result. About 2,500 years ago the country was largely peat. Compaction, oxidation and digging, all driven by drainage, have left about 2,733 km², 10% of its land. Draining peat also destroys the habitat of many species.

soil-class-075.title: Peat fires that smoulder underground for years
soil-class-075.text: A fire in peat can outlast the season, the year, even the century. Peat fires burn in peat deposits and smoulder underground for long periods, and light rain does not put them out. Peat's high carbon content lets it burn once dry. A wildfire reaching below the surface can ignite it. Then it smoulders, creeping undetected through the ground for months, years or even centuries. Fire is not wholly foreign to peat bogs. Bogs burn naturally and depend on wildfires to stop woody plants from lowering the water table and shading out bog plants. The damage comes at scale. In 1997 peat and forest fires in Indonesia released between 0.81 and 2.57 gigatonnes of carbon, equal to 13–40% of the carbon from global fossil fuel burning. A 2010 heat wave of up to 40 °C ignited peat in Central Russia. In June 2019 Arctic peat fires emitted 50 megatonnes of CO2. Climate change now makes such fires much more likely than before.

soil-class-071.title: How stalled decay builds a bog
soil-class-071.text: Peat is what happens when rot stalls. Peat formation is the build-up of plant material that fails to decay fully under acidic, oxygen-poor, waterlogged conditions, the setting described in {{ref:soil-chem-125}}. Most of the material comes from bog plants such as mosses, sedges and shrubs. The process feeds itself. Accumulating peat holds water, so conditions slowly grow wetter and the bog spreads. Sphagnum is especially good at this. It secretes tannins that preserve organic material, and its water-holding hyaline cells keep the bog constantly wet. Most modern peat bogs formed 12,000 years ago at high latitudes, after the glaciers retreated at the end of the last ice age. Growth is slow, usually about a millimeter a year. Boreal peat bogs therefore take thousands of years to reach their average depth of 1.5 to 2.3 m. The result is a vast store of carbon: an estimated 415 gigatonnes in the north, 50 Gt in the tropics and 15 Gt in South America.

soil-class-060.title: Serpentine soil, where heavy metals rule
soil-class-060.text: Some soils are poisoned by their own bedrock. Serpentine soil is an uncommon soil formed from weathered ultramafic rock, such as peridotite and serpentinite, rock in which iron or magnesium minerals make up more than 70%. Its minerals belong to the serpentine group: antigorite, lizardite and chrysotile, or white asbestos. Serpentinite forms when olivine-rich peridotite reacts with water, mostly in oceanic crust near mid-ocean ridges. The terrain is steep, rocky and prone to erosion, so the soils stay shallow, and sparse plant cover leaves them hot and dry. They hold little organic matter, nitrogen, phosphorus or potassium, and too little calcium for their magnesium. High chromium, iron, cobalt and nickel make them poor for farming. Adding gypsum or other soluble calcium fixes the ratio enough for crops and pasture. These soils occur from the Balkans, Cyprus and the Alps to Cuba and New Caledonia, and most North American ones are in California. Dust from the crushed rock carries asbestos, a health hazard.

soil-class-048.title: Brown earth, the easy farmland of temperate lands
soil-class-048.text: Brown earths cover 45% of England and Wales. These well-drained, fertile soils of humid temperate climates lie mostly between 35° and 55° north. The largest expanses lie in western and central Europe, Russia, eastern North America and eastern Asia. They form where rainfall is moderate, usually below 76 cm a year, and their pH runs from 5.0 to 6.5. Soil organisms and roots mix mull humus into the mineral matter, building a brownish A horizon over 20 cm deep with a blurred lower edge. Below lies a lighter B horizon of weathered parent material. Limited leaching moves only the more soluble bases down. Rust-like iron oxides give the rich color, and the B horizon lacks the gray colors and mottles of gley soils. Permeable and easy to work most of the year, brown earths are prized for farming, and much of their deciduous woodland has been cleared. The WRB calls them Cambisols, and German taxonomy calls them Braunerde.

soil-class-083.title: Charcoal, wood baked without air
soil-class-083.text: Charcoal is what remains when wood or other plant and animal material is strongly heated with little oxygen. Water and volatile compounds are driven off, leaving a lightweight black carbon residue. Traditional burners built a kiln or conical pile that burned part of its own wood to char the rest. Modern retorts do the job more efficiently. Large-scale production has long driven deforestation, particularly in Central Europe. Research on {{ref:soil-class-053}}, an Amazonian dark soil, revived charcoal in horticulture. Growers use it to improve soils and to lock away carbon. {{ref:soil-fert-050}} is a form of charcoal, sometimes modified, meant for uses such as adding to soil.

soil-class-053.title: Terra preta, the black soil people made in the Amazon
soil-class-053.text: Clear a patch of Amazon forest and rain or flooding soon strips the soil of its nutrients. Yet scattered through the basin lie patches of soil that stay dark and fertile. This is terra preta, a human-made {{ref:soil-class-120}}. Pre-Columbian farming communities created it between 450 BCE and 950 CE. They added charcoal, bones, broken pottery, {{ref:soil-fert-028}} and {{ref:soil-fert-023}} to poor Amazonian soil. Weathered charcoal gives the black color. Charcoal from {{ref:soil-fert-087}} stays in the soil for thousands of years, binding minerals and nutrients, so terra preta resists leaching. It holds on average three times the organic matter of the soils around it, up to 150 g/kg, and phosphorus reaches 200–400 mg/kg. Its A horizon holds more than 13–14% organic matter, and the soil can reach 2 m deep. It is reported to regenerate at 1 cm a year. The WRB calls it Pretic Anthrosol, and most began as Ferralsol. Around it lies infertile terra comum, mainly Acrisols, Ferralsols and Arenosols. Lighter, brownish terra mulata, the farmed land around settlements, falls in between for fertility. Its extent is uncertain. Estimates run from 0.1–0.3% of low forested Amazonia, or 6,300 to 18,900 square kilometers, to 10% or more, and model-based predictions put it at 3.2% of the forest. Plots average 20 hectares.

soil-class-050.title: Rendzina, the thin dark soil on limestone
soil-class-050.text: On limestone slopes the soil can be little more than a dark skin over broken rock. Rendzina is a shallow, humus-rich soil formed on carbonate-rich, or occasionally sulfate-rich, parent rock, recognized in British, German and some older classifications. Limestone is by far the commonest base, but rendzinas also form on dolomite, gypsum, marble, chalk and {{ref:soil-fert-079}}, typically on slopes in karst and mountain landscapes. Water carrying dissolved carbon dioxide dissolves the carbonate and carries it away. Insoluble clay minerals stay behind in the upper soil. There, organisms build humus, and the clay protects it from further decay; together they give dark colors and crumb structure. In Wales the profile is simply dark calcareous topsoil straight onto shattered limestone. Calcium and magnesium are plentiful, but potassium is often low. Rendzinas are a passing stage. Once they lose their carbonate they become another soil, unless erosion keeps stripping soil away. Shallow and sloping, they store little water, so they often keep semi-natural vegetation.

soil-class-073.title: Peat archives, a diary kept in layers
soil-class-073.text: Peat keeps a diary. Because it builds up over thousands of years, its layers preserve pollen, spores, plants, animals and archaeological remains, letting scientists reconstruct past vegetation, climate and land use. Harry Godwin, a scientist of peat bogs, coined the phrase peat archives in 1981. Researchers compare peat records with modern bogs to gauge how people have changed the movement of mercury. They date the layers by methods such as the vertical spread of lead-210. Acidic, tanning water and an antibiotic called sphagnan preserve bog bodies almost perfectly, such as Denmark's Tollund Man, who lived in the 4th century BC.

soil-class-077.title: Burning peat for heat, power and whisky
soil-class-077.text: For centuries people warmed their homes with the ground itself. Peat fuel is dried peat burned for heat and power, traditionally cut by hand and left to dry in the sun. In Ireland and Scotland stacked peat fed cooking fires and home heating, a tradition traced to the Roman period. Ireland's state-owned Bord na Móna milled peat for power stations and sold peat briquettes for homes. In 1929 peat supplied over 40% of the Soviet Union's electricity, falling to 1% by 1980. Some Scotch whisky distilleries, such as those on Islay, dry malted barley over peat fires.

soil-class-076.title: Peat hags, the overhanging banks of eroding bogs
soil-class-076.text: In damaged peat the ground can break into steep banks capped by an overhanging lip of plants. These are peat hags, a form of erosion at the sides of gullies cut into peat. They form when flowing water cuts down into the peat, or when fire or heavy grazing exposes its surface. Exposed peat then wears away further under wind, water and livestock. The banks are too steep and unstable for plants to take hold, so they keep eroding unless restored.

soil-class-078.title: Gardening without peat
soil-class-078.text: Peat has long filled garden pots, but that is changing. Peat in horticulture means its use as a raw material for gardening, now restricted in some places. In 1999 the UK set its horticulture industry a target of 90% peat-free by 2010. Kew Gardens has discouraged peat as a soil additive since 2003, and the Royal Horticultural Society promotes peat-free gardening. Peat-free mixes based on bark and coir are rising in the UK, while other European countries, Canada and parts of the US still use peat. Chile has forbidden peat extraction since April 2024. Peat grow cups have about 4.5 times the carbon footprint of single-use plastic cups.

soil-class-072.title: Fibric, hemic, sapric: grading peat by decay
soil-class-072.text: Not all peat has rotted equally. Soil scientists divide peat material into three kinds by how far it has decomposed. Fibric peat is the least decomposed and consists of intact fiber. Hemic peat is partly decomposed. Sapric peat is the most decomposed of all. The source plants matter too. Phragmites peat, made of reed grass and other grasses, is denser than many other kinds.

soil-class-080.title: Frozen peat and the carbon it guards
soil-class-080.text: Around half the area of northern peat bogs is frozen year-round. This peatland permafrost covers about a tenth of all permafrost area and holds about a tenth of permafrost carbon, 185 ± 66 Gt. Dry peat insulates well, with a thermal conductivity of around 0.25 W m−1 K−1. It shields the frozen ground from thaw, forming raised features called palsas and peat plateaus. Thaw tends to raise methane emissions while only slightly increasing CO2 uptake, so it adds to the warming feedback from thawing permafrost carbon. Under 2 °C of global warming, 0.7 million km² of peatland permafrost could thaw.

soil-class-079.title: Rewetting a peatland back to life
soil-class-079.text: A drained bog can often be healed by blocking its ditches. Peatland restoration repairs damaged peat bogs, usually by blocking drainage channels so they rewet and native vegetation recovers. Rewetting limits carbon release in the short term. Later, the new vegetation supplies the litter that restarts peat formation. Actively reintroducing bog plants re-establishes typical communities within 5 years, helping animals, insects and birds return. Pools add microhabitats and raise the variety of life. The Convention on Biological Diversity names peat areas as key ecosystems to protect, and wet habitats in general are also protected under the 1971 Ramsar Convention.

soil-class-051.title: Terra rossa, the red soil of Mediterranean karst
soil-class-051.text: Across the Mediterranean, a rust-colored soil lies in patches over limestone. Terra rossa is a well-drained, reddish, clayey to silty soil of neutral pH. It covers limestone and dolomite bedrock in karst regions as a discontinuous layer from a few centimeters to several meters thick. Its red comes from hematite forming in preference to goethite. For a clay-rich soil it drains surprisingly well, because the karstic rock beneath gives it high internal drainage and a neutral pH. That drainage makes it popular for wine, in La Mancha in Spain and in Coonawarra and the Barossa Valley in Australia. Soils of this red Mediterranean kind developed fastest from the Miocene to the Late Pleistocene, during large climate swings. The 1938 USDA taxonomy described terra rossa as deep, red and formed under higher rainfall than rendzina. Systems such as the FAO's formally replaced the class, but it is still in common use, and as of 1997 it remained in Israel's and Italy's national classifications. Its equivalents are chromic Luvisols on the UNESCO/FAO world map and rhodustalfs in USDA soil taxonomy.

soil-class-057.title: Dark earth, the soil left by centuries of settlement
soil-class-057.text: Dark earth is an organic-rich layer up to 1 m thick that, in geology and archaeology, marks long-lasting human settlement. Charcoal gives its color, and it may hold fragments of pottery, tile, animal bone and other artifacts. It is read as soil enriched with sooty remains of thatch from chimneyless houses and other waste. In England it covers many areas built up in the Roman period, especially Londinium, between deposits dated to the 2nd–5th centuries and the 9th century. Archaeologists first called London's layer 'black earth', then renamed it to avoid confusion with chernozem, whose color is traditionally put down to humus rather than soot. They still disagree whether it records Roman refuse or gardening, a population decline, or deposits formed after the city was abandoned. For at least 700 years West African farmers have built their own dark earth around their towns with rotted kitchen, animal, farm and fire waste.

soil-class-054.title: Why Amazonian charcoal still feeds the soil
soil-class-054.text: The charcoal in terra preta was not just any charcoal. Indigenous farmers added low-temperature charcoal, a form of pyrogenic or black carbon, to poor soils. Some terra preta holds up to 9% black carbon against 0.5% in the soils around it, and other measurements found carbon 70 times higher than in nearby Ferralsols. Poly-condensed aromatic groups, tightly bonded ring structures of carbon, keep it stable against microbes for thousands of years. Slow oxidation creates carboxylic groups that raise the soil's cation exchange capacity. Its pores hold organic matter, water and dissolved nutrients, and pollutants such as pesticides too. Low-temperature charcoal carries an inner layer of condensates that bacteria consume; charring at high temperature burns it off and adds little fertility. Fresh charcoal must first be charged with nutrients, for example by soaking two to four weeks in a liquid nutrient, or it briefly depletes available nutrients. The earthworm Pontoscolex corethrurus eats charcoal and mixes it, finely ground, into the mineral soil.

soil-class-084.title: Fill dirt, the earth used to raise the ground
soil-class-084.text: Kansai International Airport stands on a new island of fill about five square kilometers in area. Fill dirt is earthy material used to fill a hole or depression, build mounds or otherwise change the level of land. It is usually subsoil and the parent material beneath, with little organic matter or life. Rotting organic matter leaves voids that let fill settle and damage structures on top. Most is mined from sand and gravel pits to an engineer's grading specifications. Common uses include building up highway shoulders and raising low construction sites against flooding.
